summary: Develops and tests a richer shared language for the capabilities students build through their course and wider King’s experience, using the UK Standard Skills Classification as the leading candidate and moving from discovery through deep trailblazer adoption before any institution-wide skills architecture is settled.
detailSummary:
King’s has an opportunity to move beyond narrow graduate attribute frameworks and give every student a richer, more personal and more usable account of what they can do. The UK Standard Skills Classification is a strategically attractive leading candidate because it connects thousands of skills with knowledge, tasks and occupations, but its richness also creates real questions about complexity, higher-education fit, external traction and usability. King’s should therefore test it seriously rather than presume adoption.

Year 1 will concentrate first on the curriculum-facing problem. King’s will test whether technology can reliably surface meaningful capabilities from real educational evidence, what source material is rich enough to support that work, and whether the classification can represent disciplinary and higher-order learning without creating excessive noise. Student, academic and external-user testing will examine whether a mediated King’s experience makes the language useful rather than exposing end users to the raw framework.

If the approach proves promising, King’s will build capability with a small number of willing trailblazer programmes, departments or faculties prepared to go all in: making capabilities visible in curriculum and learning design, using the language with students, and exposing the operational and academic work required. Portability testing will then determine what can travel beyond unusually committed settings before a shared architecture is institutionalised through Curriculum Framework review, the wider opportunity ecology and the Digital Student Experience Hub.

The enduring ambition remains a living student skills profile through which students can recognise and evidence capabilities, connect them with purpose and possible futures and make intentional choices about development. Programmes and opportunities can contribute context about where capabilities may be encountered, practised and demonstrated, while the eventual evidence and trust model distinguishes association, student claim, student evidence and institutional assurance rather than treating programme mapping as proof that every student possesses a skill.
problemSolved: Generic graduate attribute frameworks leave too much skills development implicit, flatten disciplinary difference and give students insufficiently detailed language for understanding or using what they have developed. King’s also lacks evidence that a more granular external classification can yet solve that problem at higher-education scale without becoming too complex or burdensome.
whatChanges: King’s develops a tested shared skills architecture that preserves individual and disciplinary richness, makes capability development more visible and intentional and can connect curriculum, wider opportunities, student purpose, evidence and future possibilities. The institutional architecture is adopted only after discovery and trailblazer evidence establish what is useful and portable.

caseForChange.problem:
Universities commonly reduce the complex and individual learning gains of higher education to short frameworks of generic graduate attributes. These frameworks tend to reproduce similar claims about critical thinking, collaboration, communication and creativity. They are often internally celebratory, reasserting what a university education says it provides without offering sufficient detail for students to understand or use those gains.

Their breadth makes them difficult to operationalise or assure. Graduate attributes frequently appear in programme validation and marketing but remain peripheral to the lived student experience. Mapping an attribute to a programme can create an assumption that its students possess it regardless of the paths they take, the learning design they actually encounter or what each person can credibly demonstrate.

This leaves too much skills development implicit, obscures disciplinary difference, encourages faculties to create competing frameworks and provides a weak basis for dialogue with employers and occupations. Students are left to translate between institutional, disciplinary and external languages without a sufficiently detailed account of their own development.

A more granular framework is not automatically the answer. The UK Standard Skills Classification is rich but complex, and King’s does not yet know whether it can be mediated successfully for higher education, whether the available curriculum evidence is rich enough for reliable mapping, or whether the resulting language will be useful to students, academics and external audiences.
caseForChange.opportunity:
The UK Standard Skills Classification provides a detailed national language connecting skills with knowledge, tasks and occupations and is the leading candidate for a King’s skills architecture. King’s can test whether it provides enough external coherence and granularity to overcome the limitations of generic attributes while developing a mediated King’s experience that protects users from unnecessary complexity.

Discovery can test three linked questions: whether the classification is fit for higher education and where it needs curation or extension; whether technology can reliably help surface capabilities; and what educational evidence is needed to make mapping credible. This can produce a shared evidence semantics that distinguishes where a capability may be encountered from what a student claims, evidences or King’s is willing to assure.

King’s can then build capability with a small number of willing trailblazer disciplines, programmes or faculties prepared to use the approach deeply in curriculum and student practice. Their work can show what changes in learning design, assessment, academic practice and student support are actually required. Portability testing can distinguish what relied on exceptional local commitment from what is realistic as a common institutional architecture.

If the approach survives that testing, programmes and disciplines can express distinctive combinations of capabilities without creating separate and incompatible languages. Students can connect capabilities with their purposes and possible futures without needing a fixed occupational destination. The resulting language can connect curriculum, wider experiences, recognition, microcredentials and graduate articulation, while King's can contribute credible practical insight to the national skills agenda.
caseForChange.whyNow:
A central threat to the graduate premium is growing doubt about the relevance of degree-level education to employment and a rapidly changing economy. Academic courses do not need to become training for a single occupation, but King’s does need better ways to make the capabilities developed through disciplinary learning visible without collapsing that learning into a short generic list.

The launch and continuing development of the UK Standard Skills Classification creates a timely opportunity to test a more detailed national language while there is still scope for higher education to influence how it is applied. At the same time, Curriculum Framework review is being designed now and interested faculties are already considering their own approaches to skills. King’s needs enough common direction to prevent avoidable fragmentation without imposing an untested central framework.

The Digital Student Experience Hub also creates a future route to make skills information usable for students, but the raw classification and current curriculum evidence are not yet ready to be encoded at scale. Deliberate Year 1 discovery therefore reduces the risk of building an institution-wide skills experience around assumptions that have not been tested.

Now is the right time to investigate seriously, build evidence and hold the institutional space for a shared approach; it is not yet the right time to declare the final architecture settled.
caseForChange.intendedChange:
King’s establishes a tested living skills language used at course and student level. Every student can build and revisit a skills profile connected to their purposes and future possibilities, with clear distinctions between capabilities associated with experiences, student claims, student-provided evidence and institutional assurance.

Programmes and wider opportunities make capability development more visible and intentional, while disciplines retain the ability to express their distinctive combinations within a shared institutional architecture. Students can understand transferability as something they actively build and carry across contexts rather than as a generic list attached to their degree.

The resulting language can travel across curriculum, wider experiences, recognition and future possibilities. It enables King’s to identify recurring or signature features through aggregation while preserving the richness of individual and disciplinary learning. The architecture that becomes institutional is the one that has survived discovery, deep trailblazer use and portability testing.
